intro: The stage on which Firishta's history unfolds — cities, frontiers, rivers and holy places. 'Now' is the modern location, 'read' is where the place matters most in the volume. The 1768 spellings (Ghizni, Moultan, Sumnat &c.) are kept; the Editor's note gives the modern reading.

places.name: Ghizni
places.book: The 'Empire of Ghizni' of Part II: seat of Sabuktigin's slaves, of Mahmud's minting, and of the golden throne whose mosque threshold received fragments of the Somnath idol.
places.note: Today a small Afghan city, Ghazni was briefly one of the great cultural and military capitals of Asia under Mahmud — a centre of Persian poetry and the springboard for seventeen raids into India.

places.name: Hindostan
places.book: The whole stage: 'the History of the Hindoos before the first invasion… by the Mahomedans.' The name colours every page, from the fabulous kings to the eve of Timur.
places.note: In Dow's and Firishta's usage 'Hindostan' specifically meant northern India — the basins of the Indus and Ganges — not the peninsula (the 'Decan'), which the Delhi sultans only intermittently reached.

places.name: Delhi
places.role: Capital of the Sultanate; a city of seven successive capitals
places.book: Three Delhis meet here: the 'old city' of the Chauhans, the palace of Seri (Siri, Alauddin's city) and Firose-abad — the stage for the Slave, Khalji and Tughlaq sultans, and finally the two kings warring within one capital.
places.note: By the late 14th century Sultanate Delhi sprawled across several walled cities. Timur, entering in 1398, is reported to have been astonished by the gardens — and to have depopulated the city in three days of massacre.

places.name: Moultan
places.book: Time and again the hinge of war: besieged six months by Timur's grandson, contested between the Tughlaq governors, and the refuge of princes and pretenders throughout Part III.
places.note: Multan, on the ancient trade route to Central Asia, has been a fortified prize for millennia — one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of the subcontinent and, then, a stronghold of Sunni learning.

places.name: Lahore
places.role: Ghaznavid frontier capital; refuge of defeated sultans
places.book: Where Muhammad Ghori recovered from his wound after the first Tarain defeat, and where pretenders and exiles repeatedly gathered armies to march on Delhi.
places.note: Lahore was Mahmud's winter capital and, for the Ghaznavids, the western seat from which India was governed — a role the city would replay for empires for nine hundred years.

places.name: Sumnat
places.role: The great temple destroyed by Mahmud (c. 1025/26)
places.book: The sea-girt 'lofty castle on a narrow peninsula' and the richest idol of Hindostan — whose destruction, Dow reports from Firishta, yielded treasure 'greater… than any royal treasury ever contained.'
places.note: Somnath has been destroyed and rebuilt many times over a millennium; a temple stands there today. Modern historians debate the raid's scale but not its reality — it remains one of the most contested events in Indian historiography.

places.name: The field of Tarain
places.role: Scene of the two decisive battles (1191 & 1192)
places.book: Dow places it near 'Tannassar' on the 'Sirfutti' (Saraswati) river — first a Rajput victory, then, on the same field, the ruin of Pittu Rai's army of 300,000.
places.note: Tarain (Taraori) is one of the pivot-stones of Indian history: the second battle ended Hindu supremacy over the north and opened it to the Delhi Sultanate.

places.name: Ajmere
places.role: Capital of Prithviraj and the Chauhans
places.book: Where Ghori sent his embassy 'with a declaration of war if they should reject the true faith', and whose fall — with 'thousands put to the sword' and the rest enslaved — followed the second battle of Tarain.
places.note: Ajmer was a Rajput stronghold on the trade route to the west; its conquest, like Tarain, brought Rajputana within reach of Delhi — an omen of the long struggle between the sultans and the great Rajput house of Mewar.

places.name: Tiberhind
places.role: The frontier fort of Razia's imprisonment and marriage
places.book: The fort to which the great Empress Rizia was sent after her army's mutiny — and where her captor and jailer Altunia married her, the strange alliance that twice marched on Delhi to win back her empire.
places.note: A minor fort on the desert frontier of Punjab, Tabarhinda enters history almost solely through Razia's last, doomed campaigns — a footnote fort made famous by a queen's fall.

places.name: The river Sind
places.role: The great western barrier of Hindostan
places.book: The crossing-point of every invader from the north-west — Mahmud's armies, Ghori's, and finally Timur, whose crossing of the Sind is the last line of Vol. I.
places.note: Few rivers have been crossed by so many world-conquerors. The Indus was the pivot of Dow's whole scheme: everything east of it was 'Hindostan', and to cross it was to enter the history of India.

places.name: The Cheiber Pass
places.book: Mentioned as the 'fort of Cheiber in the passes of the mountains' built by the Afghan-Pathan tribes to guard the approaches of Hindostan — a barrier every north-western invader ultimately had to force.
places.note: The Khyber has funneled armies for over two thousand years — Alexander, Mahmud, Ghori, Babur, and later the British — making it the single most strategic defile in the region's history.

places.name: Sirindiep
places.role: The island refuge of the Somnath garrison
places.book: Where the four thousand of Somnath's garrison fled by boat 'intending to proceed to the island of Sirindiep' after their walls fell — Dow's footnote glosses it simply: 'Ceylon.'
places.note: That defeated defenders of a temple in Gujarat would sail for Sri Lanka tells us how far Arab and Indian maritime trade had knit the Indian Ocean together by the 11th century.

places.name: The Ganges
places.role: The sacred river of the Hindoos
places.book: Mentioned with awe at Somnath — the idolaters washed the god 'every morning and evening, with fresh water from the Ganges, though that river is above five hundred crores distant.'
places.note: The water for the daily bath came from thousands of miles away — a measure both of the Ganges' sanctity and of the immense pilgrim routes that already crossed India in the 11th century.
